newsitem.title: USA: Clinton agressively seeks votes in Florida.
newsitem.headline: Clinton agressively seeks votes in Florida.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, bouyed by strong economic data and his own surge in opinion polls, campaigned on Friday in a conservative region of Florida in a bid to end the Republicans recent White House winning streak there.

Welcomed by chants of "Four more years" to start a rally that was broadcast live on local television, Clinton became the first Democratic presidential contender to stump in an area traditionally considered a hopeless cause for the party.

Hoping to end a two-decade-old Republican stranglehold over Florida's presidential voting, Clinton ended a two-day swing through the state that stressed his record on the economy, education, the environment and health care -- issues where he has a solid edge over Republican rival Bob Dole.
"America is on the right track for the 21st Century," Clinton told the crowd, noting the just-released data by the Labour Department shows that unemployment has fallen to 5.1 percent last month.

The decline in the unemployment rate, which was especially steep among workers over 55 and in their early 20s, brought the jobless rate to its lowest level since March 1989 when it was 5 percent, the department said.
With a series of new nationwide polls showing Clinton with a growing double-digit lead over his Republican challenger, the Democratic incumbent publicly cautioned his followers against complacency.
"Let me assure you, we are not taking anyone or anyone's vote for granted," he said during a speech in Orlando to delegates at the National Baptist Convention, an 8 million- member black group.
"We know that the only poll that counts is the one they take on November the fifth," Clinton told the highly partisan audience. "I ask you to remember that and help others remember it as well."

In appearances in Panama City -- a traditionally conservative area of the state that gave him little support four years ago -- and in Orlando he celebrated the jobless rate as vindication for his policies.

"The American economy, my fellow Americans, is on the right track and we need to keep it going in that direction," said Clinton, who contends that the 15 percent across-the-board tax cut advocated by Dole would only reverse the nation's economic progress.

Clinton campaign officials privately have worried that overconfidence could undermine their efforts as the Nov. 5 election nears -- particularly now that some of the inroads Dole made at the time of last month's Republican convention have been eroding.

A Washington Post-ABC News poll published on Friday gave Clinton a lead of 51 percent to 37 percent over Dole, while a New York Times-CBS News survey the same day put the margin at 50 to 35 percent in favour of the incumbent.

A nationwide poll taken for Reuters found broad-based support for Clinton over his Republican rival on a series of issues that potential voters said were important to them. The poll, conducted by John Zogby International, found that on education issues 55.4 percent of voters favoured Clinton, 25.4 percent backed Dole and 6.2 percent trusted Texas billionaire Ross Perot, the Reform Party candidate.

On health care, Clinton was favoured by 48.7 percent to 27.7 percent for Dole, while Perot trailed with 5.2 percent. Clinton held a similar wide lead on dealing with environmental issues, with 51.1 percent of voters comfortable with him while 19.2 percent chose Dole. Perot was backed by 3.2 percent.
